newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine says West interested in non-nuclear zone.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine says West interested in non-nuclear zone.

text.p: Foreign Minister Hennady Udovenko said on Friday that Western countries were ready to discuss Ukraine's proposal to establish a non-nuclear zone in Central and Eastern Europe.

Udovenko also said his former Soviet republic, one of the most active participants in NATO's "Partnership for Peace" programme, wanted to reach a deal to create a "special partnership" with the alliance.

"I sent letters to the foreign ministers of 16 NATO countries and to NATO Secretary General Javier Solana and asked that this be discussed," Udovenko told a news conference after returning from the U.N. General Assembly in New York.
He said U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott, French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette and German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel indicated that they were prepared to discuss the notion.
"We have received their answers. These letters were very serious," he said. "They did not reject the idea and showed they were ready for talks."
President Leonid Kuchma initiated the idea of a non-nuclear zone this year in response to fears that potential new members of NATO would deploy NATO nuclear arms on their territory.
Non-nuclear zones already exist in Antarctica, Southeast Asia, Africa and the Caribbean.

The Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland are seen as the most likely initial candidates to join NATO, which says it has no immediate plans to station nuclear weapons in eastern Europe in the event of expansion.
Kuchma and other Ukrainian leaders have ruled out NATO membership for the moment but called for a closer relationship between Kiev and the alliance.
Udovenko said Ukraine favoured the stand adopted by NATO states like Norway and Denmark, which became members on the clear understanding that nuclear arms would not be based on their territory.
Ukraine, which once held more than 1,800 nuclear warheads, transferred the last of its share of the former Soviet nuclear arsenal to Russia for dismantling on July 31.
Unlike Russia and Belarus, it says it understands the desire of eastern European states to join NATO and says no country is entitled to block another state's membership bid.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin said this week NATO would have to negotiate a new relationship with Moscow before proceeding with expansion.
